reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A structured-lending unit's year, JPY bn: revenues 14.0, direct costs 2.5, funding transfer charge 8.0, expected credit loss 1.2. Its economic capital of 12.0 earns the 1.0% JGB risk-free rate. Tax rate 30%. The pack also lists regulatory capital (16.0) and a 0.9 trading VaR, which are not part of this numerator.
ask: After-tax risk-adjusted income (the RAROC numerator) is:

options.label: JPY 2.42bn
options.why: Stopped before the tax step: $14.0 - 2.5 - 8.0 - 1.2 + 0.12 = 2.42$ is pre-tax, and the numerator is after tax.

options.label: JPY 1.61bn
options.why: Left out the return on economic capital: $(14.0 - 2.5 - 8.0 - 1.2) \times 0.7 = 1.61$. The capital buffer earns $r_f \times EC = 0.12$, which is added back.

options.label: JPY 7.29bn
options.why: Forgot the 8.0 funding transfer charge, so the income is overstated by $8.0 \times 0.7 = 5.6$.

takeaway: RAROC numerator: revenue less costs, funding and expected loss, plus the return on economic capital, then taxed. Divide by economic capital (12.0) for 14.1%.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A SGD 800m corporate loan portfolio yields 8.5%, with direct costs of SGD 7m a year. It is funded by deposits transfer-priced at 5.5%. Expected loss is 0.8% of the portfolio a year. Economic capital is 6% of the portfolio, held in government bonds yielding 4%. Tax rate 25%; after-tax hurdle rate 12%.
ask: Compared with zero, the portfolio's NIACC (after-tax income less the hurdle charge on economic capital) is:

options.label: Negative
options.why: Divided after-tax income by the SGD 800m portfolio instead of the SGD 48m of economic capital, getting about 1.2% against a 12% hurdle. The hurdle is a return on capital.

takeaway: Hurdle comparisons are on economic capital: RAROC is 9.39/48 = 19.6%, well above 12%, so NIACC is positive (about SGD 3.6m).

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A bank sets one firm-wide hurdle rate as the weighted average of its cost of common equity (CAPM, beta 1.2, risk-free 4%, market return 10%) and its cost of preferred equity (7.0% yield). Common equity: market value CAD 6.0bn, book value CAD 3.0bn. Preferred: market value CAD 1.5bn. Tax rate 25%.
ask: The weight on common equity in the blend is closest to:

options.why: Used the book value of common (3.0) against the preferred (1.5): $3.0/4.5 = 67\%$. Weights come from market values, $6.0/7.5$.
Put the book value of common over the market total: $3.0/7.5 = 40\%$. Numerator and denominator must both be market values.

takeaway: Capital-structure weights are market values. With 80% common at 11.2% and 20% preferred at 7.0%, the hurdle is 10.36%, between the two costs.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: To find the break-even revenue on a CAD 500m loan book we work backwards. Economic capital is CAD 40m, the hurdle rate is 12% after tax, and the tax rate is 28%. Direct costs are CAD 4m a year, funding is at 4.5%, expected loss 0.6% a year, and the capital earns 3.5% in government bonds.
ask: The pre-tax risk-adjusted income the book needs so that the after-tax return just equals the hurdle is closest to:

options.label: CAD 4.80m
options.why: Treated the after-tax hurdle charge $12\% \times 40$ as if it were pre-tax. It must be grossed up for the 28% tax.

options.label: CAD 3.46m
options.why: Multiplied by $(1 - 0.28)$ instead of dividing: tax makes the required pre-tax figure larger than 4.80, not smaller.

takeaway: Working back from a required after-tax figure, divide by $(1 - t)$. Pre-tax income must exceed the after-tax hurdle charge.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: An equipment-leasing activity has an expected after-tax RAROC of 12.4%. The bank's traditional hurdle is 10.5%, the risk-free rate 3.0% and the expected market return 8.0%. The activity passes the adjusted-RAROC test while $\text{RAROC} - \beta_E (R_M - r_f) > r_f$.
ask: The highest equity beta at which it still passes is closest to:

options.why: Compared RAROC with the traditional 10.5% hurdle instead of $r_f$: $(12.4 - 10.5)/5.0 = 0.38$. The adjusted test is against the risk-free rate.
Scale slip: divided the 9.4 points by 0.5 instead of 5.0 (premium misread by a factor of 10).
Mixed units: divided 9.4 percentage points by the premium as a decimal (0.05), without converting 9.4% to 0.094.

takeaway: Adjusted RAROC charges shareholders $\beta (R_M - r_f)$ and demands what is left exceed $r_f$. Break-even beta is (RAROC - r_f) over the market premium.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: A Basel II Foundation IRB bank computes capital for a JPY 50bn senior unsecured loan to a highly rated Japanese corporate. Its own estimates are PD 0.01% and LGD 30%. Under Foundation IRB the supervisor sets a floor on corporate PDs and fixes LGD for senior unsecured claims.
ask: The PD and LGD that go into the capital formula are:

options.label: PD 0.01%, LGD 30%
options.why: Used the bank's own estimates for both. That is Advanced IRB; under Foundation the bank supplies only PD, and even that is floored.

options.label: PD 0.03%, LGD 30%
options.why: Applied the PD floor but kept the internal LGD. Foundation IRB uses the supervisory 45% for senior unsecured claims.

options.label: PD 0.01%, LGD 45%
options.why: Took the supervisory LGD but forgot the 0.03% floor on corporate PDs, so the 0.01% estimate is raised.

takeaway: Foundation IRB: own PD (floored at 0.03% for corporates), supervisory LGD 45% for senior unsecured, supervisory maturity of 2.5 years.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel 2.5 market-risk capital, one-day 99% figures in CAD m. VaR: yesterday 6.5, 60-day average 1.6. Stressed VaR: yesterday 7.4, 60-day average 6.9. Four backtesting exceptions in 250 days give a multiplier of 3 on both. Each term is the larger of yesterday's figure and 3 times its average. The two are added and scaled to ten days by the square root of time.
ask: The market-risk capital charge is closest to:

options.label: CAD 27.2m
options.why: Left out the ten-day scaling: $6.5 + 20.7 = 27.2$ is still a one-day figure.

options.label: CAD 272m
options.why: Scaled by 10 days instead of $\sqrt{10}$: $27.2 \times 10 = 272$.

options.label: CAD 860m
options.why: Scale slip (10x): applied the ten-day scaling twice, as $27.2 \times 10 \times \sqrt{10}$.

takeaway: Scale one-day figures to ten days with the square root of time (about 3.16), not by 10. The larger-of rule can bind on either the latest figure or the multiplied average.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: NSFR build for a bank, funding in CAD m with ASF factors: stable retail deposits 620 (95%), 3-month wholesale CDs 240 (0%), 10-year senior bonds 180 (100%), common equity 110 (100%).

options.label: CAD 1,150m
options.why: Added the amounts without the ASF factors. Short-term CDs count for nothing and retail deposits only 95%.

options.label: CAD 910m
options.why: Left the retail deposits at 100% instead of 95%: $620 + 180 + 110 = 910$.

takeaway: ASF = sum of funding x its factor. Against required stable funding of 725, NSFR is 879/725, about 121%.

reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
setup: A bank's available stable funding is SGD 630m against required stable funding of SGD 675m (NSFR 93%), a gap of SGD 45m. It will raise new stable retail deposits (ASF factor 95%) and invest all the proceeds in own-sovereign debt (RSF factor 5%) until NSFR is exactly 100%.
ask: The new deposits needed, compared with the SGD 45m gap, are:

options.label: Less than SGD 45m
options.why: That needs each SGD raised to add more than SGD 1 of net stable funding. It adds 0.95 of ASF and also creates 0.05 of required funding, so it adds only 0.90.

options.label: Exactly SGD 45m
options.why: Treated each SGD raised as closing SGD 1 of the gap, ignoring both the 95% ASF factor and the 5% RSF on the new sovereign debt.

takeaway: New funding closes an NSFR gap net of what it adds to required funding. Each SGD of deposits closes only about 0.90, so the need exceeds the gap.

reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
setup: Output floor, EUR bn. Modelled RWA: credit 480, counterparty 60, CVA 30, market 62, operational 70 (total 702). Standardised-only RWA: credit 760, counterparty 90, CVA 30, market 80, operational 70 (total 1,030). The fully phased-in floor is 72.5% of the standardised total, applied to total RWA.
ask: After the floor, total RWA is:

options.label: Unchanged at EUR 702bn
options.why: Applied the floor to one line only: $72.5\% \times 760 = 551$ looks slack against 480-702. The floor is on the total, $72.5\% \times 1{,}030 = 747$.

takeaway: The output floor is on total RWA: modelled RWA at 68% of the standardised total sit below 72.5%, so the floor binds and adds about EUR 45bn.

reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
setup: Output floor phase-in for 2026: the floor is 70% of standardised-only RWA. The supervisor caps the increase in RWA caused by the floor at 25% of RWA before the floor. A bank has RWA of EUR 80bn on its approved approaches and EUR 150bn on standardised approaches only.

options.label: EUR 80bn
options.why: Ignored the floor altogether. At 70% of 150 the floor is 105, above 80.

options.label: EUR 105bn
options.why: Applied the floor but not the cap. The increase 25 exceeds the allowed 25% of 80, which is 20.

options.label: EUR 108.75bn
options.why: Used the fully phased-in 72.5% instead of the 70% for 2026, and skipped the cap.

takeaway: With a cap, RWA = min(floored RWA, 1.25 x pre-floor RWA). Check the floor first, then the cap.

setup: A bank wants its economic capital to cover unexpected losses at a confidence level matched to a target credit rating. That rating has a one-year default probability of 0.07%. The next rating up has 0.03%.
ask: The confidence level to use is:

options.why: Used the default probability of the next rating up (0.03%). The target rating's own 0.07% sets the level.
Percent slip: subtracted 0.07 from 1 as if it were 7%, giving 93%.

takeaway: Confidence level = 1 minus the default probability of the target rating. A better rating means a higher confidence level and more capital.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A leveraged fund holds economic capital equal to the worst-case loss at 99.5% confidence minus expected loss. Expected loss is USD 50m and unchanged. The worst-case loss rises from USD 500m to USD 1bn.
ask: The increase in economic capital is:

options.label: Smaller than USD 500m
options.why: Deducted the USD 50m expected loss from the change, getting 450. Expected loss is deducted from both levels and cancels in the difference.

options.label: Larger than USD 500m
options.why: Reported the new capital level of USD 950m rather than the increase.

takeaway: A constant deduction cancels in a change: the move in economic capital equals the move in worst-case loss.

reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
setup: A credit portfolio has a loan-equivalent exposure of USD 480m. Expected loss is 1.0% of exposure and is already covered by pricing and loan-loss reserves. The worst-case loss at the bank's confidence level is 3.0% of exposure.
ask: Economic capital to attribute, as a percentage of exposure, is:

options.why: Took the whole worst-case loss as capital. The 1.0% expected loss is covered by pricing and reserves, so it is deducted.
Took the expected loss itself as the capital. Capital covers the unexpected part, not the expected loss.
Added the expected loss to the worst-case loss instead of subtracting it.

takeaway: Economic capital = worst-case loss minus expected loss, here 2.0% of USD 480m = USD 9.6m.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel I. Bank A has capital of USD 10m (Tier 1 6 plus Tier 2 4). Assets: USD 50m claim on an OECD bank (20% weight), USD 100m corporate loans (100%), USD 40m uninsured residential mortgages (50%).

options.label: USD 190m
options.why: Added the assets at face value with no weights.

options.label: USD 150m
options.why: Gave the mortgages 100% instead of 50%: $10 + 100 + 40 = 150$.

takeaway: RWA is the weighted sum, 130. The capital ratio is then 10/130 = 7.7%, below the 8% minimum.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel I. A bank holds USD 1.5bn of loans to corporations, of which USD 600m is commercial real estate, plus USD 300m of OECD government claims and USD 500m of cash. Weights: 0% for cash and OECD government, 50% for uninsured residential mortgages, 100% for all other claims.
ask: Risk-weighted assets, compared with the USD 1.5bn of corporate loans, are:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Gave the USD 600m of commercial real estate the 50% weight, which applies to residential mortgages only: $900 + 300 = 1{,}200$.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Weighted the OECD government claims and cash above 0%. They carry 0%, so they add nothing.

takeaway: Basel I relief for property applies to residential mortgages only. Commercial real estate is an 'other claim' at 100%.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel I current exposure method. A EUR 1bn interest-rate swap has more than five years left (add-on 1.5% of notional) and is currently worth -EUR 2m to the bank. The counterparty is a corporate, weighted at 50%.
ask: The swap's credit equivalent amount, compared with the EUR 15m add-on, is:

options.label: Less than the add-on
options.why: Netted the negative value against the add-on: $15 - 2 = 13$. Current exposure is $\max(V, 0)$, so a loss to the bank counts as zero.

options.label: More than the add-on
options.why: Added the size of the negative value, $2 + 15 = 17$. The bank loses nothing today if the counterparty defaults.

takeaway: Credit equivalent amount = max(V, 0) + add-on. A negative mark adds nothing and also does not reduce the add-on.

reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
setup: Basel I current exposure method. A USD 200m interest-rate swap has six years left and is worth +USD 3.5m to the bank. The add-on for interest-rate contracts over five years is 1.5% of notional. The counterparty is an OECD bank at a 20% risk weight.
ask: The swap's risk-weighted asset amount is closest to:

options.label: USD 0.13m
options.why: Scale slip (1/10): the correct 1.3 divided by 10.

options.label: USD 6.5m
options.why: Stopped at the credit equivalent amount $3.5 + 3.0 = 6.5$ and never applied the 20% risk weight.

options.label: USD 61m
options.why: Percent as decimal: used an add-on of 1.5 times notional (300) instead of 1.5%, so $(3.5 + 300) \times 20\% = 60.7$.

takeaway: Derivative RWA = (max(V, 0) + add-on) x counterparty weight: the credit equivalent amount is not yet the RWA.
